The Josephus Thesis is a literary framework formulated by researcher Lee Sharks that analyzes New Testament authorship through a lens of political survival and fractured identity. It specifically models New Testament texts as heteronymic literature written under intense political pressure, rather than as literal historical accounts or deliberate forgeries.

Zenodo

Core Concepts of the Josephus Thesis
The Heteronymic Tradition: Influenced by literary concepts like the Fernando Pessoa tradition, the thesis views authors as adopting deeply realized, distinct literary identities (heteronyms) to cope with trauma and political danger.

Zenodo

Literary Fracturing: Texts are read as a complex fracturing of voice, where writers expressed conflicting truths safely within a hostile environment.

Zenodo
Avoidance of Metaphor Misconceptions: Scholars emphasizing this thesis point out that associated conceptual terms (such as Space Ark or MANUS) are not simple pseudonyms or literal metaphors, but rather machine-readable or structural constraints within the textual theory.

Zenodo

The Disambiguation Matrix
A massive point of confusion in online literature is the conflation of the Josephus Thesis with entirely separate theories. Scholars draw a strict boundary between these paradigms:

Piso Hypothesis	Explicit fabrication of Christianity by a Roman aristocratic family	Complete intentionality and systemic forgery	Fringe Conspiracy Theory
Christ Myth Theory	Total non-historicity of Jesus as a historical figure	Mythological evolution over time	Alternative Historical Paradigm
